blocks.text: This small parish (*freguesia*) lies between the parishes of São Jorge and Boaventura, about six kilometres from the parish church of the former and approximately two from that of the latter.

The shape of the hills surrounding it sufficiently explains the name it retains. It belonged to the parish of São Jorge from its creation in 1517 until it was separated from it in 1676. It therefore quite naturally took the name Arco de São Jorge, which long predates the parish’s creation.

Pedro Gomes Galdo, one of Madeira’s earliest settlers, held extensive lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Jorge and Boaventura. We may presume that these included the lands which later formed the parish of Arco de São Jorge. We cannot know when Arco began to be settled or when its lands first began to be cleared, but it seems to us that this occurred towards the end of the 15th century or in the first quarter of the 16th century, well before the parish of São Jorge was created.

On the spot now occupied by the locality (*sítio*) of Casais there once stood a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity). The year of its foundation is unknown, but we presume that it must date from the third or last quarter of the 16th century. It had its own chaplain, who conducted religious services there under the authority of the vicar of São Jorge. This chapel became the seat of the new parish, created by the diocesan prelate Dom Antonio Teles da Silva under the authority granted by the royal decree (*alvará régio*) of Peter II dated 28 December 1676.

Long before the parish was created, the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade was already in a lamentable state of repair and threatened with imminent collapse. Only ten years after it became the parish seat, Bishop Dom Estevão Brioso de Figueiredo visited it in person and ordered that an application be made for the immediate construction of a new church. He considered the small chapel too cramped and unfit to serve as the parish church. It was not until half a century later, by order of the Council of the Exchequer (*Conselho de Fazenda*) dated 18 January 1740, that construction of the new church was ordered. It was blessed on 19 March 1744 by the vicar at that time, Father Manuel da Costa.

We know that Fathers João Batista and José de Andrade served as chaplains of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade before the parish was created, and that the latter priest was the first to perform the duties of parish priest there. He was succeeded as pastor of souls by Fathers Francisco da Costa, Francisco Manuel Pereira, Bartolomeu Marques Caldeira, Joaquim Baptista Catanho, Bernardo Ribeiro, etc.

blocks.text: This small parish is perhaps the most fertile on the whole north coast of the island. It produces every kind of agricultural crop, and its land is particularly well suited to growing sugar cane. Its output would, however, be greater were irrigation water not scarce. A considerable portion of its land is cultivated only with cereals and vegetables, and even these crops are left dependent on rainfall. To remedy these drawbacks, it is essential to build a levada (irrigation channel) beginning in the locality of Falca, in the parish of Boaventura, to irrigate extensive areas of land in that parish and also in Arco de São Jorge. The surveys and related plans were completed more than thirty years ago, when the works were estimated to cost around thirty *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis). In the legislative session of 1890, the deputy Canon Feliciano João Teixeira advocated this important improvement before the national assembly. The works were never begun, however, and the construction of the levada remained merely a proposal.

The fertility of this parish’s soil is matched by its healthy conditions and mild climate. The mortality rate is low, and epidemics that have occurred on Madeira, such as the cholera outbreak of 1856, have not reached it. Its climate is among the mildest and most temperate on the entire north coast. High mountains shelter the settlement from the harsh, biting winter winds, although this does not rule out the possibility of common diseases and even epidemics appearing in this parish, as they do everywhere. We therefore know that in 1768 a disease of an epidemic character spread there and caused many deaths. On that occasion, Antonio Rodrigues Seabra, the surgeon of the parish of Boaventura, rendered outstanding service, while the parish church fabric provided substantial donations to combat the epidemic. Another disease appeared in this parish in 1849. It was then classified as diarrhoea and killed many people, while countless others were affected. The district’s civil governor at the time, the beneficent Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council), went there in person, accompanied by two physicians and carrying the essential resources needed to treat the sick. The disease was eradicated within a short time. (See *Epocha Administrativa*, vol. 2, p. 506 ff.).

blocks.text: The principal localities in this parish are Igreja, Casais, Lagoa, Poços, Arco Pequeno and Quebrada. The last owes its name to the great landslide (*quebrada*) that fell there more than two centuries ago, breaking away large tracts of land, chiefly from Arco Pequeno, which formed that locality. Such events are common in Madeira: the parish of Jardim do Mar, part of the parish of Paul, the locality of Lugar de Baixo and others were formed in the same way. At Quebrada do Arco de São Jorge, however, a most remarkable circumstance occurred. It deserves special mention, and we have found several references to it, including in Dr Pereira Drumond’s *Noticias Mineralogicas da Ilha da Madeira*, published in 1818 in the *Investigador Portuguez*, and in works by other Portuguese and foreign authors. These accounts agree perfectly with local tradition, which still preserves the memory of the event intact. Interesting details of this extraordinary occurrence are found in a letter discovered in 1848 at the Public Library of Lisbon (*Biblioteca Pública de Lisboa*) by General Antonio Pedro de Azevedo. Some years ago, the following curious extract from it was published in a Funchal newspaper, and we reproduce it here. (See *Verdade*, no. 944): ‘I give Your Mercy this news because it is a marvellous event. On the far side of the island, at Arco de São Jorge, most of which is an estate belonging to my entail (*morgado*), the ground had for many years lain open with a great fissure. As the land was very steep, after the severe winter weather this year, at midnight on Easter Day, a great mass of earth ran out into the sea for about half a *légua*, carrying the rocks and shoals before it so gently that the houses, trees and trellises remained standing; in one place, two casks of wine resting under the canteiro system (natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating) did not overturn; a beehive upon a slab did not fall; and a hen brooding over eggs, tethered at the foot of a fig tree, was found there. Everything remained unchanged, and the ground was not broken up. It formed an island in the sea measuring about twenty *moios* of sowing land, which is joined to this land. It created a beach with two fine harbours, which were needed in that area because nothing could be embarked there on account of the shoals. Where the land had run away, it left a hollow above with a sheer cliff and, below, a *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) of excellent new soil extending until it meets the land in the sea; previously there had been a very high cliff where the land met the sea. It moved without a crash and without being noticed, except by one man who, seeing it moving at night, suffered a fit. It was like a boat being launched into the sea, running upon skids. The marvel is that, for several days beforehand, throughout the width of the land that moved, the tide neither rose nor fell for three days, and the sea was as though dead, while on either side it ebbed and flowed with the waves customary in the northern sea.’
This occurred in 1689 and, if it took place on Easter Sunday as the letter states, it must have been on 20 April of that year.

blocks.text: The most distinguished son of this parish was Antonio Gil Gomes, whom we shall discuss at greater length in the relevant entry. Antonio Januario Moderno was also born there, on 25 February 1789, the son of Captain João Rodrigues Moderno and Dona Antonia da Incarnação Moderno. He was superintendent (*provedor*) of Machico, which then included the municipality (*concelho*) of Sant’Ana, and held other public offices. In his day he was renowned throughout Madeira, not only for the eccentric and hospitable way in which he received guests at his home in Arco, but above all for his Herculean physical strength. He was feared and respected for the many remarkable feats and acts of courage he performed. In London, where he lived as a political exile, he also became known among his compatriots for his courage and the strength of his arm. He died in Funchal on 11 October 1864. His son was Dr Antonio Januario Moderno, who graduated in medicine from a foreign university and practised with great success and skill in the United States, where he acquired a large fortune. He too was born in the parish of Arco de São Jorge. He spent almost his entire life outside Madeira, but died in this city around thirty years ago, shortly after returning to his native land. He had earned a reputation as a man of exceptional talent and a distinguished physician. He died in Funchal on 11 February 1885, aged 67.

The distinguished priest Antonio Alexandrino de Vasconcelos was born in the parish of Boaventura in 1791, but lived in Arco de São Jorge for more than forty consecutive years and died there in 1884. He was vicar general of the bishopric and held other important offices. In 1834 he accompanied the prelate Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade when the latter was forced into exile and left for Italy. He was a clergyman of remarkable intelligence and learning and was considered a great authority on the various branches of Catholic liturgy.

The patron saint of this parish was Nossa Senhora da Piedade until 1744, when St Joseph became its patron upon the construction of the new church. By the papal briefs of 24 and 26 August 1784, the altar in the chancel was declared a privileged altar, and a plenary indulgence was granted to be gained on the feast day of St Joseph. We found somewhere the curious information that Francisco Aurelio da Câmara Leme, holder of the entail, charged the freely disposable third of his estate with the perpetual obligation to provide the oil required to light the Blessed Sacrament in the church of Arco de São Jorge. His son and heir, Francisco Antonio da Câmara Leme, also holder of the entail, ratified and assumed this obligation by a public deed drawn up on 18 February 1766, with the charge falling upon ‘the *quinta* (country estate) in front of Santo Amaro’.

Among the rural parishes of Madeira outside the seats of their municipalities, Arco de São Jorge still had, only a few years ago, the lowest rate of illiteracy, which, as is well known, is so deeply and regrettably rooted among us. This was due to the zeal with which several parish priests provided primary education there. Special mention should be made of Father Isilio Joaquim Vares in the second quarter of the 19th century and, subsequently, Fathers Emilio Marques da Silva, Francisco Manuel de Sousa, Francisco Antonio de Abreu and Casimiro Augusto de Freitas. On 16 January 1886, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Sant’Ana established an official boys’ school in Arco de São Jorge, which has provided valuable service there. Several years later, this school was converted into a mixed school.

This parish belongs to the municipality of Sant’Ana and the judicial district (*comarca*) of São Vicente. It lies approximately twelve and a half kilometres from their respective administrative seats, around forty-one kilometres from Funchal by the Poiso road and thirty-seven kilometres by way of Curral das Freiras and Boaventura. Its population is 167 inhabitants. We should also mention that the celebrated popular troubadour Manuel Gonçalves was born in this parish. Known as Manuel Feiticeiro, he died a few years ago after travelling throughout Madeira singing his artless poetic compositions. These greatly delighted the crowds, who listened to him avidly and bought the dozens of pamphlets in which he collected and had printed his innumerable and imperfect songs.
See Popular Poetry.

blocks.text: The sugar industry prospered greatly here in Madeira between the 15th and 17th centuries, despite the abuses and extremely heavy taxes to which it was subject. Madeiran sugar was then known in the principal European markets. Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, well known for his generosity, once sent Pope Leo X several valuable gifts, foremost among them the Sacred College fashioned from sugar, with life-sized cardinals all made of *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures).

In the early days, the sugar cane was pressed in *alçapremas* (hand-operated lever presses) or in very rudimentary sugar mills (*engenhos*). The rollers of these mills were sometimes made from thick trunks of til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), suitably prepared.

In 1496, there was once-boiled sugar and twice-boiled sugar: the latter cost 600 réis and the former 350 réis per *arroba* (a weight of about 15 kg). Before then, each *arroba* of sugar, probably of the second quality, cost 339 réis.
The owner of a sugar mill gave the Infante, Lord of the Island, one third of the sugar produced; the owner of an *alçaprema* gave only one and a half *arrobas* of that product each month.
Shortly after 1452, there was only one water-powered sugar mill in Funchal, while the number of *alçapremas* was considerable because they were subject to a less burdensome tax.
The original charter (*foral*), perhaps granted by Afonso V, required sugar mills to pay one third and also obliged them to surrender half of any sugar cane that was not made into sugar.

Over time, the area devoted to sugar cultivation increased, owing to the construction of levadas (irrigation channels) to irrigate the land. Meanwhile, the contribution levied on sugar mills fell to one quarter and then to a fifth (*quinto*, a levy of one fifth on sugar). As a result, the number of these establishments grew. Together with the *alçapremas*, they produced more than 120,000 *arrobas* around 1498 and more than 300,000 *arrobas* of sugar by the middle of the 16th century.
This sugar was consumed in Madeira, Portugal and many foreign countries. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 26 August 1503 abolished the restrictions previously imposed on its export.

The royal decree of 22 March 1498 allowed foreigners to reside permanently on the island, a right denied to them by the regulations (*regimento*) of 7 October 1496. The charter of 21 January 1511 also permitted these foreigners to load consignments of sugar for export.
This sugar had to be cleared through the customs houses; from 1512 onwards, customs clearance took place solely at the Funchal customs house.

blocks.text: In 1507, sugar cost 315 réis per *arroba*, and in 1511 it cost 300 réis. The influx of sugar from Brazil and the Spanish colonies in America into European markets was the chief cause of the decline of Madeira’s sugar industry. Madeira was still exporting some sugar in 1612, but by 1649 many of its mills lay in ruins, and few remained in 1730.

In 1736, Madeira began importing this commodity from abroad and continued to do so, on a greater or lesser scale, until sugar cultivation was restored after the vineyards had been destroyed by *Oidium Tuckery*.

Between 1823 and 1826, Madeira produced an insignificant quantity of sugar, but by 1861 output stood at 275,802 kilograms. Between 1870 and 1873, annual production rose to between 800,000 and 900,000 kilograms. In more recent years, sugar was produced in the following quantities:

The colonial sugar imported by the island is not included in these figures. Local consumption amounted to 1,102,545 kilograms of sugar in 1908; 837,500 kilograms in 1912; 1,656,310 kilograms in 1916, with surplus production exported to Portugal; and 3,069,143 kilograms in 1938, while 399,780 kilograms were exported to mainland Portugal.

According to Dr Azevedo, Madeira’s modern sugar exports began in 1854. They grew rapidly from 1858, reaching their highest level in 1871 and 1872: 561,837 kilograms in the first year and 567,526 kilograms in the second. They immediately fell by half in 1873 and declined increasingly until 1881. The old manufacturers said that 100 kilograms of Bourbon cane, which was exceptionally rich in sugar, yielded about 7 to 9 kilograms of sugar, despite the very rudimentary production methods then used. Today, it is known that the average sugar yield of Yuba cane varies between 9 and 101, a fact attributable chiefly to improvements in the production methods employed.

blocks.text: Under Madeira’s sugar regime (*regime sacarino*, the legal framework governing sugar production), the price of sugar is set according to the price of cane. First-quality sugar, which in 1914 sold for 29 centavos, rose to 31 centavos the following year and then successively increased until it reached 36 centavos per kilogram. In 1900, this sugar sold for 26.5 to 27.5 centavos, while many years earlier its price had ranged between 20 and 24 centavos per kilogram. In 1939, it costs 4.20 escudos at the factory and 4.40 escudos in retail shops.

Second-quality sugar, which sold for 24 and 25 centavos per kilogram in 1910, cost 28 centavos in 1914, subsequently rising to 30 and finally 33 centavos. Before the war, this sugar was sold to the refineries in Lisbon for 18 and 19 centavos per kilogram.

Sugar is manufactured by the Fábrica do Torreão. Decree no. 23,847 of 14 May 1934, referring to Decree no. 16,003 of 29 October 1928, stipulates that until 1953, or until justified by increased consumption, no new sugar or alcohol factories may be built, the production capacity of the existing factory may not be increased and a factory used solely as a distillery may not be adapted to manufacture sugar. All the factories may, however, make the necessary machinery improvements in accordance with the law.

Since 1935, sugar production has in principle been restricted to local consumption. As this limitation is combined with the obligation to purchase all cane of a specified grade, the regime in force has thereby guaranteed the Madeiran market to the industry. If there is a surplus of sugar in any production year, up to a maximum of 200 tonnes may be shipped to mainland Portugal duty-free. Larger exports have, however, already been permitted exceptionally, for special reasons concerning the interests of agriculture and industry.
See Spirit, Alcohol, Sugar Cane and Sugar Protectionism.

blocks.text: João Gonçalves Zargo was a Homeric figure at the dawn of our maritime ventures and voyages. He led the most important discovery made by Portuguese seamen in the first quarter of the 15th century, under the fruitful and glorious guidance of Prince Henry the Navigator. The discovery of Madeira is the great, immortal monument that truly marks the auspicious beginning of our navigators’ odyssey. It represents not only a remarkable expansion of our nation’s territories, but above all our first great conquest as navigators and future masters of the seas.

The name of the illustrious navigator is inextricably linked to this momentous event in our history. The influence that this great discovery exerted on the continuation of our maritime ventures has not been given due prominence, but there can be no doubt that it was exceedingly significant. The discoverer and first coloniser of Madeira deserves a prominent place in the most brilliant pages of our maritime chronicles.

Gonçalo Velho Cabral, who discovered the islands of São Miguel and Santa Maria, achieved a more illustrious name in history because a distinguished biographer wrote a detailed portrait of him as a navigator. He devoted extensive historical research to it, with the painstaking care of a descendant who takes pride in his ancestral lineage and extols the exploits of his forebears. João Gonçalves Zargo had no descendant to write his biography, nor was any research into him conducted in the public archives beyond the little that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo found in documents kept in this city’s municipal registry. Consequently, there is a remarkable scarcity of reports and information about the great navigator. It is therefore extremely difficult to make even a modest biographical attempt in which the most characteristic features of his career as a warrior, navigator and coloniser are at least outlined in broad terms (1921).

Zarco or Zargo? The learned commentator on Frutuoso, who was also a distinguished philologist, answered this question by saying that the first is the most authentic spelling of this surname and is supported by the most reputable authors, but that it became obsolete and usage adopted the second. We consulted the earliest chroniclers and writers who dealt, however briefly, with the discoverer of our archipelago, including Gomes Eanes de Zurara, João de Barros and Damião de Góis. We found that they all wrote Zarco and that the same spelling was adopted in the accounts of the voyages made by Diogo Gomes, a contemporary of Prince Henry the Navigator, and by Alvise Cadamosto (1450). A royal letter (*carta régia*) issued by Afonso V in 1449 contains the highly archaic form Zarquo, corresponding to Zarco, the form adopted by our early chroniclers. The renowned historian of the islands, who wrote his work in the last quarter of the 16th century, uses the already modernised form Zargo. The spelling Zarco, found in two or three passages of the *Saudades*, must be regarded as a copyist’s slip or a printing error, since Gaspar Frutuoso writes Zargo many dozens and perhaps hundreds of times. This was also the spelling invariably adopted by the annotator of that work. Every consideration therefore suggests that the spelling to be used today should be that employed by the illustrious author of *Saudades da Terra* and his learned commentator.

What is the origin of the surname Zarco or Zargo, used by the illustrious discoverer of Madeira? João de Barros and then Damião de Góis, followed by Gaspar Frutuoso, the chronicler of the islands, said that Zarco or Zargo was a nickname arising from a heroic deed performed by the navigator, rather than a surname inherited from his noble ancestry. The learned annotator of the *Saudades* does not share the chroniclers’ opinion. He says that the versions given by Frutuoso cannot be accepted as true and are merely another example of the general method used to invent legends: to personify and break down into a more or less plausible fable a proper name whose origin is unknown. To support his assertion, he cites several early books of nobility in which the discoverer’s ancestors bear the surname Zarco or Zargo.

It will not be entirely out of place to relate here, albeit very briefly, the versions given by Gaspar Frutuoso and mentioned above. During one of our clashes in Morocco, a Moor who was a bold and skilful horseman challenged one of the Portuguese warriors to a bitter fight. The Portuguese was defeated, though his supreme courage was heroically paid for with his life. Another Portuguese knight, apparently followed by several more, entered the relentless combat, and all met the same unhappy fate. The captain of our stronghold refused to allow any more lives to be sacrificed to the fierce wrath of the diabolical Moor. A knight who had not yet distinguished himself by his courage then came forward and pleaded most insistently for permission to attack the victorious Moor. Let us now hear the author of the *Saudades* in his artless and picturesque words: ‘The Soldier at once asked for the horse of a knight whom he chose for the purpose; and, mounting it with a shield on his arm and a piece of wood in his other hand, he rode towards the Moor, who, seeing him skirmishing, came at him most arrogantly. Whenever he tried to strike the Christian, the latter did no more than turn the Moor’s lance aside. He continued in this manner until, when he saw that the time and opportunity had come, he swiftly charged the Moor on horseback and struck him such a great blow while he was exposed that, having stunned him, he seized him by the hair and delivered him as a prisoner to the Captain; for this deed he was thereafter known to the King. From this valiant Soldier, they say, descended João Gonçalves the Zargo, his son or grandson; others say that João Gonçalves himself performed this feat of arms; and because the Moor whom he, his father or his grandfather killed was called Zargo, the same surname and name remained with them, or with him.’

Our first conquest in Africa took place in 1415 and Madeira was discovered four or five years later, so it is difficult to believe that the discoverer’s grandfather, who must already have been well advanced in years at the time, could have been the hero of that feat. It would be more credible to attribute it to his father, and still more so to the navigator himself. Yet even the chronicler seems not to have regarded the account as particularly credible, for he adds these words to his narrative: ‘The information I have from the island of Madeira tells of this beginning in another way:...’. Immediately afterwards, he tells us that during the siege of Tangier, ‘Zargo proved himself so knightly that he demonstrated his great courage, fighting valiantly before the Infantes, who therefore held him in high esteem. At this place and in this battle, he received a wound in one eye from a crossbow bolt shot at him by the enemy, which destroyed that eye. Since at that time anyone with only one eye was called *zargo*, the name remained with him as an emblem and honour of his knighthood; for he gave such proof of it and distinguished himself so greatly as a knight that his courage and skill in war contributed considerably to enabling Prince Henry the Navigator to escape and withdraw to the sea, by which time Infante Ferdinand had already been taken captive through treachery and cunning, as is related at length in the *Chronica d’El-Rey D. Duarte*’.

Friar Francisco Brandão says in the *Monarchia Lusitana*: ‘There is no reason to accept the explanation given by Dr Gaspar Fructuoso in his history of the Islands, where he says that.... Zarco was so nicknamed because he was blind in one eye or because in Africa he had killed a Moor called Zarco....’.

Still concerning the origin of the discoverer’s surname, one of the notes to *Saudades* reproduces the following passage from a genealogical work by José Freire Monterroio Mascarenhas: ‘The Zarco family is almost as old as the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), for records of it have been found in its archives since the 12th century. Although we know that there is a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) in the province of Alemtejo, near the town (*vila*) of Viana do Alentejo, named Zarco, it has always seemed to us that the family did not take its surname from that place and that the surname arose not from a manor house but from a nickname. This is because the word *Zarco*, in both Castilian and Portuguese, means a man with greenish eyes, which Antonio de Nebrixa renders in Latin in his *Diccionário* with the word *glaucus*. Jeronymo Cardoso says the same in his *Vocabulário*, as does Ambrosio Calepino in his *Diccionario*. It was therefore given as a nickname to one person, from whom it passed as a surname to his descendants’.

blocks.text: The birthplace of João Gonçalves Zargo remains unknown to us. Dr Alvaro de Azevedo says ‘that authors disagree about his birthplace: some maintain that he was born in Tomar, because the Zargo family had an estate there, as the chronicler Brandão states; others say Lisbon; and some Matosinhos or Porto, where Lousada says that the Zargos had a chapel.

Some old Madeiran genealogies state that Zargo was born in Matosinhos, and the writer Francisco Manuel de Melo, a descendant of the discoverer, also says that he was born in that locality. The third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the discoverer’s grandson, relinquished his captaincy and settled in Matosinhos, where he died in 1530 (volume I, page 207). It has been conjectured that he withdrew to this part of mainland Portugal because he may have come from there, because of family traditions or because of property owned there by his family. None of these reasons provides conclusive proof that the great navigator was born in Matosinhos, but they are certainly presumptions worthy of the fullest consideration. We should add that only recently we were assured that the locality still preserves a tradition that the discoverer of this archipelago was born there.

What was the precise date of his birth? One of the notes to Frutuoso’s work states: ‘It is not known for certain in which years João Gonsalves Zarco lived. From the fact that he was a young man in 1419, and that his firstborn son, João Gonçalves da Câmara, died aged eighty-seven in ... March 1501, and was therefore born in 1414, we infer that Zargo was born around 1395’. It seems to us that Zargo’s birth should be dated to shortly after 1390, which would mean that he was between 25 and 30 at the time of the discovery. Some chroniclers described him then as a young man, still not far advanced in years, although we must not forget that he had already distinguished himself as a navigator and had conducted himself heroically during the second siege of Ceuta.

If we are to credit the genealogist Freire Mascarenhas, already cited, João Gonçalves Zarco was the son of Gonçalo Esteves Zarco and Dona Brites, daughter of João Afonso of Santarém, comptroller of the household of King John I. Gonçalo Esteves, who lived during the reigns of Afonso IV, Peter I and Ferdinand I, was the son of Estevão Pires Zarco, who styled himself Advocate in the King’s Household and held important judicial offices.

Although the glory surrounding the name of the navigator Gonçalves Zargo is not enhanced by his having illustrious ancestors and belonging to a family with noble traditions – something which, in those days, was nevertheless of paramount importance – truth requires us to say that the discoverer of the archipelago came from noble stock and, as such, attended the household of Prince Henry the Navigator as one of its members. This is stated by the old chroniclers Eanes de Azurara and João de Barros, confirmed by the historian of the islands and also recorded in the oldest and most reputable Madeiran genealogies. A genealogy of Zargo appears in a book of nobility by José Freire Monterroio de Mascarenhas, already cited above, whose manuscript is held in the Lisbon Public Library. It traces the illustrious navigator’s known ancestors back to the 12th century. In our view, one of the fullest proofs of his noble origins is his marriage to Dona Constança Rodrigues de Sá, daughter of Rodrigo Aires de Sá, who represented Portugal in Rome and there married Dona Cecilia Colona, daughter of the Marquis and Prince of Colona, a member of one of the oldest, noblest and most highly regarded families of the Roman patriciate. This has only now been confirmed to us by an illustrious researcher from mainland Portugal, after several investigations into old and authoritative documents (1921). It should be noted that a marriage contracted in such circumstances at that time, when Zargo had not yet achieved renown as a celebrated discoverer and was not yet the wealthy captain-donatary of Funchal, could have taken place only if the bridegroom were a man of rank and proven noble ancestry. Aires de Sá, who misses no opportunity to praise the merits of the discoverer of the Azores in extravagant terms and who at times refers to the discoverer of Madeira with manifest injustice, says that João Gonçalves Zargo ‘was a man of modest origins ... who managed to rise within the Household of Prince Henry the Navigator and who developed into a settler’. The truth, however, is that he offers no evidence to support his claim, which is moreover directly contradicted by the chroniclers, the genealogies and the customs of the period.

blocks.text: The genealogist Freire Monterroio, cited above, says that Gonçalves Zargo began ‘to serve Prince Henry the Navigator when still very young’, and thus underwent lengthy training in the school of that illustrious and worthy prince. Zargo distinguished himself as a navigator, making several voyages along the African coast, which was then the tried apprenticeship – the arduous, practical course – of our daring seafarers. Some writers, including Francisco Manuel de Melo, assert that the illustrious navigator was the first to introduce artillery aboard his vessels, and that this improvement in the art of warfare at sea was therefore due to his inventive genius and martial ardour. He served as captain of the Algarve coast and fought several engagements at sea against Moors and Castilians, always displaying exceptional courage.

The discoverer of Madeira also distinguished himself as a brave and daring soldier, and the chronicles left us highly laudatory accounts of his heroic conduct at Ceuta and Tangier. He was knighted in the former stronghold. During the disastrous campaign at Tangier, he did much to ensure that Prince Henry the Navigator could embark under cover from the Moors’ attacks. Frutuoso writes on this subject: ‘Through the skill and valour of this knight, João Gonçalves Zargo, Prince Henry the Navigator withdrew and embarked aboard the ships waiting at sea for that purpose. Zarco remained ashore throughout, gathering together as many men as he could and valiantly withstanding the onslaught and force of the Moors who were bearing down upon him to prevent the Prince from embarking. After the men had withdrawn, with the loss of many Portuguese, João Gonçalves himself withdrew, badly wounded and amid hardship and danger, for the Moors were countless. For this great service rendered to the Prince by the magnanimous João Gonçalves Zargo, and for others that he had rendered to the King, he was held in high esteem; the King entrusted him with offices of great responsibility, in which he always proved himself a most gallant knight.’ His descendants continued the glorious traditions of their forebear, for many of them, particularly his successors in the captaincy, distinguished themselves by their valour in the fortified towns of Africa, as we have already noted in the articles devoted to them in the first volume of this work (1921).

Shortly after the discovery of this archipelago and the division of its captaincies, Gonçalves Zargo settled in Funchal with his wife and children and began the work of settling and colonising his donatary captaincy (*donataria*). ‘Captain João Gonçalves Zargo’, says *Saudades*, ‘sheltered his ships by the islets off the cape of this place, where there was a beautiful cove, and resolved to build his wooden residence ashore. He promptly built it beside the sea, on high ground, where the captain’s wife (*capitoa*, wife of the captain-donatary), Constança Rodrigues, later founded the chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria).’ It was beside this small place of worship that Zargo had his first residence: undoubtedly a more than modest and uncomfortable single-storey wooden dwelling, entirely devoid of architectural embellishment, like all the earliest houses built here in Madeira.

We have already said elsewhere that it was from the secluded retreat of Santa Catarina that Zargo directed the initial work of colonisation and laid the foundations of the future town (*vila*), which advanced rapidly and achieved remarkable development during his lifetime. There he may have dreamt of the progress of the captaincy, of which he was the donatary (*donatário*), and of the advancement of the house he had founded, foreseeing in the near future the honours and privileges that would be lavished upon his descendants and successors. He may perhaps have divined that the monarch would reward him with the insignia of nobility and the right to bear a coat of arms, already envisioning his grandchildren’s pedigrees adorned with the coronets of counts and grandees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), in tribute to the services rendered by their grandfather...

Some years later, the discoverer moved his residence to the left bank of the stream, at the foot of the hill later named Pico dos Frias and near the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), which he had built there and dedicated to St Paul. It is said that this was the first stone residence built in Funchal.

His final home, where he spent most of his life, stood very near the site on which he had the church of Conceição de Cima built. An old manuscript states: ‘He also resolved to build a residence for himself, as he did on high ground overlooking the valley of Funchal, directly opposite a church of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, intended as a family vault for himself and his kin.’ This is the present-day church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), while his residence is the old manor house of the Lomelino entailed-estate holders, now known as Quinta das Cruzes. A fuller account may be found in the article *Moradias de Zargo*, on page 395 of volume II of this work, to which we refer the reader.

blocks.text: It is known that João Gonçalves Zarco devoted himself tirelessly to colonising his captaincy, whose seat rapidly grew in importance. A quarter of a century after settlement began, and during the discoverer’s lifetime, it was raised to the status of a town; approximately fifty years later, it was granted the rights of a city by a royal decree (*alvará régio*) of 21 August 1508. Little is known in detail about the government of the first donatary, but neither is anything known that reflects badly on the public administration of his captaincy. One accusation has been made against him: that he started the voracious fire which destroyed a considerable part of the original, luxuriant woodland that covered this island from the ocean shore to the mountain peaks. This episode, described at some length on page 140 of volume 2 of the *Elucidário*, was certainly a reckless undertaking whose disastrous consequences the first settlers may not have been able to assess. It is also true, however, that rapid and extensive colonisation made it imperative to clear some of those dense, impenetrable thickets, which only fire could reduce to the necessary proportions and thereby permit immediate agricultural development. According to João de Barros, the vast area over which this fire spread appears to have caused serious damage and difficulties for the early colony. It is also beyond doubt that Madeira was rapidly repopulated by forest species and was soon covered by rich and extensive vegetation. The letter of grant (*carta de doação*) by which Henry the Navigator granted João Gonçalves Zarco the captaincy of Funchal, and under which it would pass to his direct successors, dates from 1 November 1450. This letter from the Infante was confirmed by royal letters of 25 November 1451 and 16 August 1461. The privileges and prerogatives conferred by these instruments were essentially the same as those set out in the letters of grant issued to the donataries Tristão Vaz Teixeira and Bartolomeu Perestrelo. The donataries’ powers were excessively broad and even highly discretionary, since all civil and criminal jurisdiction rested with them, except for imposing the death penalty or severing a limb. They were lords of water and wind: that is, only they could own mills or watermills. The rights to produce bread and sell salt were also reserved to them. In addition, they received a tenth of the revenues intended for the Infante and held the important prerogative of distributing uncultivated land. All this provided the captains-donatary of Funchal with a very substantial annual income, making the household of the donataries of this captaincy one of the wealthiest in the country. Zarco’s 4th great-grandson and the 5th donatary was made Count of Calheta and a grandee of the realm. The donataries of Funchal built a palace in Lisbon as their residence and lived in great splendour in the capital. We have no knowledge that Gonçalves Zarco reserved any land or real property on this island for himself or his successors in the donatary captaincy. It is known, however, that he granted vast territories to his other children and sons-in-law, including that of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) at Ponta do Sol (volume II, page 277), as well as others.

Among Madeira’s first donataries, Zarco enjoyed the greatest prestige and influence. This was certainly due to his personal qualities, rather than merely to the fact that he was a person of higher standing than Tristão Vaz Teixeira, as João de Barros says in his first *Década*. The choice of captaincy already appears to indicate the superiority accorded to the donatary of Funchal. The special advantages of the seat of this donatary captaincy included its admirable location, the spaciousness of the locality (*sítio*) for the growth of a populous settlement, the breadth of its landing place, the fertility of its soil, its picturesque setting and its mild climate. Compared with these were the manifestly inferior conditions of Madeira’s other captaincy in respect of the nature of its land, climate, lack of beaches and landing places, difficulty of communication, etc. These differences leave no doubt about the preference shown to Gonçalves Zarco when the land discovered by the two navigators was divided. Later, as Funchal developed rapidly and remarkably, the influence of the donataries of this captaincy steadily increased. At times they abused that influence by extending their jurisdiction over the other donatary captaincies, plainly encroaching upon the powers of others. The disastrous administration of the captains-donatary of Machico and Porto Santo contributed considerably to this. To some extent, this was even sanctioned by the governments of mainland Portugal, which did not curb the abuses and referred to the donatary of Funchal in official documents as the captain of the island, as though the captaincy of Machico did not exist.

As noted above, João Gonçalves Zargo married Constança Rodrigues de Sá, or de Almeida, who, according to the most authoritative genealogists, was the daughter of Rodrigo Aires de Sá, Portuguese ambassador in Rome, and Cecília Colona, of the most noble Roman family of the Marquises of Colona. A heraldic article says of this family: – ‘A Roman patrician family whose origins can be traced back to Pietro de Colona, lord of a castle near Rome, who lived around 1100. His third great-grandson, Seiarra de Colona, was made a marquis in 1289, while his descendants were later made Princes of Colona and Palestrina and Grandees of Spain; among Italian families, it is one of the most illustrious in lineage....’ According to the strongest probabilities and the genealogies we have been able to consult, when the discoverer of our archipelago came to begin the work of colonisation, he brought with him his wife, Constança Rodrigues de Sá, his eldest son, João Gonçalves da Câmara, and his daughter, Helena Gonçalves da Câmara. His third child, Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, the 3rd captain-donatary of the island of São Miguel, was very probably born in Madeira. In the article Sons and Sons-in-law of Zargo (volume II, page 31), we have already discussed the discoverer’s earliest descendants, albeit briefly, and we refer our readers there. Here, however, we must correct the information concerning Garcia Gonçalves da Câmara: he was the legitimate son of João Gonçalves Zargo and Constança Rodrigues, not the illustrious navigator’s illegitimate son, as stated there. That information was taken from a less authoritative source which we then regarded as reliable. In the article Donataries, we described the immediate succession of Funchal’s captains-donatary, descended in the direct line from the discoverer until the Philippine rule, and devoted a fairly detailed separate article to each of them on pages 201 onwards of the 1st volume of this work.

Zargo had numerous and distinguished descendants, who spread throughout Madeira, the Azores, Brazil and mainland Portugal. Some of them founded illustrious titled houses. One of his descendants, the great writer Francisco Manuel de Melo, says:

‘.... João Gonsalves Zarco, a man renowned among us, for, not counting the older houses, which are not recorded because their origins are uncertain, we have had few men in Portugal with such abundant descendants. Three counts bearing this surname – Calheta, Vila Franca and Atouguia – owe their male-line descent to him..... And through marriage, 21 titles of this Kingdom descend from João Gonsalves.’ By a charter dated 4 July 1460, Afonso V granted the illustrious discoverer the right to use a coat of arms, described in the same charter as follows: ‘a black shield and, at its foot, a green mountain upon which stands a silver tower between two golden wolves...’. In this royal letter (*carta régia*), the discoverer is named João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, and his successors were to use that name. In fact, this does not appear to have happened, even in Zargo’s own case. We have already said enough about his coat of arms, the historical error found in it, the surname Câmara used by his descendants, etc., in the article Câmara, on page 198 of volume I of this *Elucidario*.

blocks.text: Gonçalves Zargo died at a very advanced age. An old manuscript gives this picturesque account: ‘He reached such an age that he had himself carried in men’s arms to be placed in the sun, which greatly strengthened him. From there he directed the affairs of his jurisdiction, governing and administering justice with his faculties intact, never experiencing the feebleness of a decrepit man.’ Some old books of genealogy give the navigator’s year of death as 1451, others as 1461 and another as 1471. Nothing certain is known about this. The year 1451 cannot be accepted because the royal letter of 4 July 1460 shows that Zargo was still alive that year. The date 1461, considered the most probable, best accords with the 40 years during which the historian of the islands states that he governed the captaincy. On the other hand, if we accept that he was born between 1390 and 1395, as we say above, we must suppose that he was between 66 and 71 years old at the time of his death. This certainly does not correspond to the great age described by the chroniclers, particularly in that period. If we accept 1471 as the year of his death and 1390 as the year of his birth, he would have reached the age of 81, fully justifying the chroniclers’ unanimous assertion regarding his decrepitude. It may also be said that he was perhaps born before 1390, in which case the dates 1451 and 1461 might also be plausible. These are mere conjectures; at present, there is no evidence that would enable us to establish precisely the year in which the great discoverer died.

‘God was pleased to take him, says the manuscript already cited, after he had governed the island.... not as its lord, but as the father and companion of all its inhabitants.’ The discoverer’s mortal remains were buried in the church of Conceição de Cima, now the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), which he had built as a family vault for himself and his descendants. Zargo’s tomb stood in the chancel, as was generally customary for the founders and patrons of churches. It is written somewhere ‘that the work was arranged so that the grave.... stood in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so high that it made the place exceptionally venerable and awe-inspiring’. It is said that, many years later, the nuns secured the removal of the imposing mausoleum, which obstructed their view of the altar. It may have been on that occasion that the ashes of the discoverer of Madeira were transferred to the family vault of his son-in-law, Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos.

We are inclined to believe that this outrage – the removal of the mausoleum and transfer of the discoverer’s mortal remains, if it did in fact occur – must have taken place during the Philippine dynasty, when the donataries of Funchal ceased to reside on the island and their role in its government became purely honorary. It is difficult to believe that they would have permitted this desecration of the grave of their illustrious ancestor and founder of the wealthy house whose benefits they enjoyed. Frutuoso’s commentator says that the sarcophagus of Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos bears an inscription in Gothic capitals, rendered illegible by wear, and that a large marble slab can be seen on the adjacent floor, bearing the following epitaph:

GRAVE OF CAPTAIN GASPAR MENDES DE UASCONSELLOS, WHICH HE ORDERED TO BE MADE FOR HIMSELF AND HIS HEIRS BECAUSE THE FIRST GRAVE SLAB PLACED HERE WAS REMOVED, AS A DESCENDANT OF THE FIRST MARTIM MENDES DE VASCONSELLOS, WHO LIES HERE AND CAME TO THIS ISLAND TO MARRY ELENA GLIZ DA CAMARA, DAUGHTER OF JOÃO GONSALVES ZARCO, ITS DISCOVERER. IT WAS MADE IN THE YEAR 1710

This epitaph makes no reference to the discoverer’s ashes, and the inscription in Gothic lettering also appears not to concern him, according to someone whom we heard attempting to decipher it. Does it refer to Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos? Some have even supposed that the slab came from Portugal and had covered the grave there of an ancestor of Zargo’s son-in-law. When the floorboards in the chancel of the church of Santa Clara were lifted in March 1919, two tombstones were discovered there, with epitaphs relating to the 2nd, 3rd and 5th captains-donatary of Funchal, as already recounted on page 217 and the following pages of volume II of this work. Nothing concerning the discoverer was found there.

blocks.text: The chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), Quinta das Cruzes and, in particular, the church of Santa Clara are modest but memorable monuments, eloquently commemorating the discoverer and the discovery of Madeira. These buildings deserve from the public authorities, especially the administrative bodies based in Funchal, the respect and veneration customarily accorded everywhere to objects and things closely associated with the lives of illustrious men. Those bodies have a most solemn duty to maintain these buildings and, as far as possible, preserve them from the ravages of time. As we have already said elsewhere in this book, this is a most fitting occasion to make special mention of João Gonçalves Zargo’s two-handed sword (*montante*), which was always kept at Quinta das Cruzes. A continuous tradition, handed down from generation to generation within the family that owned it, leaves no doubt that it belonged to the illustrious discoverer. It was always regarded as his, and the profound veneration accorded to this relic there at all times further confirms the truth of its origin. It is an ancient weapon intended to be wielded with both hands and is not distinguished by fine craftsmanship. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but it is of great worth because it has existed for more than five hundred years and, above all, because it belonged to the great navigator who discovered this archipelago. It may be the sword that Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco during his assaults against the Moors, winning fame as a valiant and daring knight. This venerable relic is now in the hands of a foreigner in this city, who preserves it with the esteem it truly deserves. It should, however, be in the possession of this city’s Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). This administrative body must arrange for its acquisition and preserve it reverently in its archives until it can be fittingly displayed in the museum of art and antiquities that must inevitably be founded in this city one day (1921).

The idea of building a monument in this city to the illustrious discoverer of Madeira is an old one, but no serious attempt was ever even begun to turn that idea into reality and thus discharge the outstanding debt to his glorious memory. In 1918, the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) commissioned the model for a statue of Zargo to be built on Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga, along the extension of Entrada da Cidade. The model, created by the distinguished Madeiran sculptor Francisco Franco, was exhibited at the Municipal Theatre (*Teatro Municipal*) on 2 March 1919. During the celebrations marking the Fifth Centenary of Madeira, the foundation stone of the monument was laid on that avenue in a ceremony of exceptional grandeur, as already described on page 163 of this volume (1921).

Outside the city, high in the mountains and overlooking the whole of Funchal, a bronze statue of João Gonçalves Zargo stands in Terreiro da Luta. It depicts the illustrious discoverer as the caravel under his command approached this then unknown island. This monument, the work of the sculptor Francisco Franco’s chisel, owes its existence entirely to the initiative of the former merchant and distinguished Madeiran, Commander Manuel Gonçalves.

In Lisbon in 1806, the Madeiran poet Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos published a poem entitled *Zargueida*. Of this work and *Georgeida*, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says: ‘He sought to sound the epic trumpet, but it is clear that this undertaking was far beyond his talent. Consequently, in the two essays he composed in that genre, he never succeeded in rising above mediocrity. Nevertheless, both contain episodes that do no discredit to his muse and may be read with pleasure.’ Of Medina e Vasconcelos’s compositions, *Zargueida* brought him the greatest renown and remains the best known of them all today. It is an epic poem in ottava rima, modelled on the classical forms of ancient epic poetry. It is divided into ten cantos and contains more than five thousand lines. It concerns João Gonçalves Zargo’s discovery of Madeira and uses the discoverer’s surname as the poem’s title. It contains a series of interesting episodes with some felicitous poetic digressions, foremost among them the legend of Robert Machin. The discovery of this island is not described until Canto X. The poem is preceded by a sonnet dedicated to Bocage, to which that eminent poet replies with another sonnet, undoubtedly the finest composition found in this volume (1921).

The preceding passages concerning Gonçalves Zargo, transcribed verbatim from the first edition of this work, should be compared with the account on pages 354 ff. of vol. I of the 1st edition. This provides fuller clarification of the subject and also corrects some assertions made at the time, especially the notes concerning the precise date of the discovery and the names of those who carried out that undertaking, whether by chance or design (see I-355). The further new information presented below is also of particular relevance to this subject.

blocks.text: The article ‘*Alguns Documentos do Mosteiro de Santa Clara do Funchal*’, published on pp. 171 ff. of volume IV of *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, seeks to establish the correct ‘spelling’ of the surname of the captain-donatary of Funchal. It argues that it should be written Zargo rather than Zarco, as it is spelt in many places. The article includes a document from 1447 in which the surname is reproduced, including in facsimile, with the spelling Zargo. One question naturally arises: during the twenty-two years between the beginning of settlement and 1447, did João Gonçalves always write his surname with a g and never with a c? Such changes in names, surnames and nicknames are not uncommon today and were even more frequent in earlier times. The document cited supports a presumption that should not be dismissed entirely, but it does not establish an indisputable claim about which no doubt is permissible.

It should be noted that Gaspar Frutuoso, author of *Saudades da Terra*, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, its illustrious commentator, and almost all the writers who have addressed the subject used the spelling Zarco rather than Zargo.

The conjectures concerning the probable year of João Gonçalves Zargo’s death were fully resolved by the evidence provided in a valuable article published in Funchal’s *Diario de Noticias* on 23 April 1927. Written by the distinguished author João Cabral do Nascimento, it proves beyond doubt that Zargo died in 1467, a valuable contribution to Madeiran history.

The aforementioned *Arquivo Histórico*, for the year 1939, published an extensive article about João Gonçalves Zargo’s two-handed sword, discussed above. It sought to disprove the prevailing belief that it had belonged to the man to whom it had been attributed for centuries, although this was not established beyond dispute. As is well known, the two-handed sword was acquired by the public-spirited industrialist Henrique Hinton, who presented it to the Funchal Municipal Museum (*Museu Municipal do Funchal*), where it is held. Of particular interest on this subject is the article published in *Diário da Madeira* on 16 November 1939, which should be consulted by readers wishing to learn more about the matter.

The fitting tribute to the memory of João Gonçalves Zargo mentioned above was fully realised on 28 May 1934, with the ceremonial unveiling of the statue built on Avenida Arriaga, as already described on p. 394 of volume II of this *Elucidário*.

blocks.text: – He was the first Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) governor to administer this archipelago. He was appointed on 15 June 1828, and on the 25th of the same month the frigate *Príncipe Real*, which was carrying him, appeared off Funchal. However, the Governor and Captain-General José Lúcio Travassos Valdez prevented him from landing. As will be seen in the article ‘Occupation of Madeira by Miguelite Troops’, after the island had been taken by the royalist forces, José Maria Monteiro landed and took office on 24 August 1828.

His term as governor was not long, but it was sadly marked by his abuses of power and the hardships he inflicted on the inhabitants of the archipelago. The ominous special judicial commission (*alçada*) that came to the island during his tenure, presided over by the high court judge (*desembargador*) Francisco António Maciel Monteiro, committed the gravest excesses. Its inquisitorial judicial inquiry (*devassa*) implicated a hundred individuals, many of whom were imprisoned and deported from the island, while a considerable number were sent to our overseas possessions. Emigration among people of every social class fleeing persecution was very substantial, particularly to England, Brazil and North America. A considerable number of public officials were dismissed, many of them being imprisoned and sent to Lisbon. (See Special Judicial Commissions.)

blocks.text: José Maria Monteiro became notorious not only for his persecution of the island’s Liberals, but also for his lack of dignity and scruples. On one occasion, he even appropriated part of the money intended to pay the troops. It is said that, during his frequent visits to the homes of the *malhados* (‘piebalds’, a nickname for the Liberals), accompanied by constables (*quadrilheiros*), he seized everything of any value that he saw. Two of his sons also distinguished themselves in these exploits and were blamed for a major theft at Quinta do Palheiro, which belonged to João de Carvalhal.

José Maria Monteiro, who was a naval captain and held a court appointment under Miguel I, left Madeira at the end of April 1830, after his successor, Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo, had already arrived. For his biography, see what we wrote on p. 113 of vol. I and p. 95 of vol. II, when discussing Colonel José António de Azevedo Lemos and Joaquim Melchior Gonçalves.

blocks.text: The Spanish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) Dom Antonio Herédia served in the army that entered Portugal in 1580 under the command of the Duke of Alba. In 1602 he came to Madeira as captain of the Castilian Garrison Company (*Companhia do Presídio Castelhano*). He subsequently became commander of the same garrison and later governed the entire archipelago in the absence of its appointed governor. He was the founder of the Herédia family in Madeira, whose last representatives were Francisco Correia Herédia, Antonio Correia Herédia and Francisco Correia Herédia, Viscount of Ribeira Brava (see those entries). Dom Antonio Herédia and his descendants became connected by marriage to the most distinguished Madeiran families. The important Britos entailed estate (*morgadio*) was incorporated into the Herédia family. Its principal seat was in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, at the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Apresentação (Our Lady of the Presentation), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears this name today. Beside it stood a large manor house, one of the largest residences outside Funchal. The house and chapel were demolished long ago.

blocks.text: He lived in Funchal around the middle of the 18th century and was, according to tradition, a wealthy man. On one occasion, he invited several friends to spend the day in a cave east of the place where the lazaretto now stands, intending to enjoy various amusements. They all died there when the ground above collapsed. The only survivor was a black man who served Dom Cosme and had been some distance from the cave; he returned to the city with news of the terrible catastrophe he had witnessed.
The site of the catastrophe is known to seafarers as the Furna de Dom Cosme.

From 1679 to 1684, Father Dom Zenóbio de Medicis, son of Dom Cosme de Medicis, studied at the Faculty of Theology of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). It is therefore reasonable to believe that the disaster occurred long before the middle of the 18th century, since it is unlikely that Dom Cosme de Medicis was still alive at that time.
It was founded in 1621 by the priest Jerónimo da Silva and stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior. See Monuments and Terreiro da Luta.

blocks.text: This distinguished lady was born in Madras, in British India, on 3 October 1840. She settled in Madeira in 1880 and two years later founded a school in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), which she named St Georges High School. It was attended by many girls from the leading families of Funchal society. After closing the school around 1892, she rebuilt the old hospital in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz with funds from charitable donations. There she admitted several patients and established a pharmacy, providing outstanding services to the sick and poor of that municipality (*concelho*). She founded a diocesan religious community which, through its hospital work and teaching in many schools scattered across several parishes, earned the highest praise and the gratitude of the people of this island.

In 1907, during a smallpox epidemic, Miss Wilson took charge of the isolation hospital established at the Gonçalo Aires Lazaretto. The circumstances were extremely grave and the most grievous consequences were feared. Yet the services rendered by that illustrious lady were so remarkable that the unfounded fears which had arisen in many minds soon disappeared, even though people were still affected by the tragic events of January 1905.

names.rendering: Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace)

blocks.text: On this subject, one of the authors of this work wrote in the former *Heraldo da Madeira*:

‘Miss Wilson devoted her boundless self-sacrifice and her great and unfailing charity to the unfortunate smallpox patients, without seeking the slightest personal advantage or the most insignificant reward. She thereby placed herself alongside the great benefactors of humanity who, doing good solely for its own sake, aspire only to the approval of their own conscience and to rewards in the life beyond the grave.

‘Alongside this incomparable charity, her most kindly heart holds such treasures of tenderness, affection and gentleness that, at the lazaretto, she is the patients’ true providence, always with the smile of hope and consolation lighting her brow.

‘In its ignorance and excessive credulity, skilfully exploited by those who should have been its true mentors and guides, the people turned the lazaretto into an Ugolino’s prison or a cave of Cacus, where patients suffered the worst abuses, ranging from outrages against their modesty to the most heinous murders. All this was nothing more than a legend, merely the subject of a despicable scheme, yet among the general public it became an unshakeable belief, an axiomatic truth that seemed impossible to dispel or destroy.

Miss Wilson had to struggle tenaciously against these deep-rooted prejudices, superstitions and fears. The first smallpox patients entered the isolation hospital only with great trepidation. Before long, however, the spell was completely broken. Those imagined horrors are gradually fading away, and at the lazaretto they found only the burning flame of charity, shining intensely within a woman’s heart.
‘Today, the spirit of goodness is there, showering benefits in abundance: a beacon of brilliant light illuminating so many minds, a rainbow of peace and hope comforting troubled hearts.’

With the establishment of the new political regime, Miss Wilson had to leave Madeira, but she returned to Funchal and died on 18 October 1916 in the former Convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena), in Câmara de Lobos. On 15 April 1939, her remains were transferred to the chantry (*capela*) in the building on Rua do Carmo that houses the headquarters of the religious congregation she had founded.

As stated above, in 1884 Mary Jane Wilson founded a diocesan religious congregation, which she named the Franciscan Sisters of Our Lady of Victories, and it received the full approval of the ecclesiastical authorities. This congregation, devoted particularly to hospital work and the elementary education of poor children, has rendered the most outstanding services here, as everyone without exception acknowledges, always with the utmost zeal and dedication. Today, the beneficial work it performs in managing the charitable institutions entrusted to it has become indispensable. A considerable number of its members are already working selflessly in the evangelical missions of Portuguese Africa.

blocks.text: In several dozen articles scattered throughout this work, particularly those on pp. 139 and 303 ff. of volume II and those mentioned there, we have dealt at some length with the industries of this archipelago. These articles would benefit from closer and more logical coordination, but pressing circumstances prevented us from arranging them as we would have wished.

As it may shed some light on these matters, we must mention the pamphlet by the writer and economist Peres Trancoso, *O Trabalho Português, I, Madeira*, published in 1929, on the sources of this archipelago’s economic wealth and its industrial and commercial development, although we may disagree with several assertions made in that work.

We wish to refer particularly to some of the conclusions presented by the author. The statistical data on which this information was based are not given, although they should have been included there or, at the very least, their authoritative and reliable source should have been cited.
The notes under the heading *Riqueza*, which we shall reproduce verbatim, are of interest:

blocks.text: With Madeira having approximately 200,000 inhabitants, individual wealth amounts to 6,670 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), or £67 in round figures. Although this is low relative to the island’s productive wealth and potential, it merely demonstrates that laws restricting income, excessive taxes and laws taxing export products, etc., impoverish the region and disrupt its natural economy. Nevertheless, the numerical conclusion is not discouraging, for the future looks bright for the beautiful island of Madeira, until one day it occupies the place that belongs to it in the Nation’s economy as a whole.

blocks.text: During the revolt that broke out in Torres Vedras on 4 February 1844, with the aim of bringing down the Costa Cabral government, 23 insurgents were arrested and sent to Madeira. They included the lawyers António Maria Ribeiro da Costa Holtreman and Leonel Tavares Cabral, Commerce Court judge Lourenço de Oliveira Grijó, Canon Dr Manuel Joaquim Cardoso Castelo Branco and eight army officers.

Some of these political prisoners came aboard the brig *Douro*, which arrived in Funchal on 20 April, and were taken to the Ilhéu fortress (*Fortaleza do Ilhéu*). The rest came aboard the cutter *Andorinha*, which arrived here on the 28th of the same month, and were confined in the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*). They were all released as soon as unofficial news reached Madeira that the Torres Vedras revolt had failed.

blocks.text: In 1919, after the monarchist revolution at the beginning of that year, new political prisoners were brought to Funchal. They arrived aboard the steamer *Africa*, belonging to the National Navigation Company (*Empresa Nacional de Navegação*), which had been converted into a military transport. The 289 prisoners, accompanied by a naval contingent, disembarked on 8 May, three days after the *Africa* had arrived, and were housed in the Gonçalo Aires Lazaretto. Among them were the former minister João de Azevedo Coutinho, the former colonel João de Almeida, the Count of Sucena, the Count of Arrochela, the Viscount of Siqueira and João Moreira de Almeida. A naval guard of 30 men and 1 sergeant remained in Funchal to guard the lazaretto, and an infantry detachment commanded by a second lieutenant joined them for the same purpose. On the orders of the harbour master, all vessels were forbidden from entering or remaining in the maritime zone between the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) and Cabo Garajau.

Despite these precautions, on 3 June it was discovered that 8 prisoners, including the Count of Sucena, had disappeared. It later became known that they had all reached Las Palmas aboard the motor launch *Glafiberta*, owned by the sportsman Humberto dos Passos, who had organised the escape. We read the following account of the escape in a newspaper: ‘One fine afternoon, nearly all the political prisoners interned at the Funchal lazaretto left the building on the pretext of getting some air and gathered on the narrow strip of beach immediately below it. The guards merely watched them from the lazaretto windows. For a while they sang, frolicked and cheered; when the uproar reached its height and the guards were distracted by the revelry, a boat dispatched from the *Glafiberta* approached the beach and unhurriedly took aboard the 8 prisoners.... Hours later, the motor launch, towed by the *Milano* of the Blandy company (which was unaware of the nature of the service requested of its tug), sailed towards the Desertas and later turned south, bound for the Canary Islands’.
The owner of the *Glafiberta* also accompanied the eight prisoners. Several days earlier, he had asked the harbour master for permission to sail his boat around the island.

Of the remaining prisoners who had been confined in the lazaretto, 7 were released following a telegram received from the Minister of War on 13 May. All the others departed for Lisbon aboard various liners that called at Funchal between June and August. The steamer *Moçambique* carried away the prisoners who were the last of the 280 to have disembarked at Funchal on 8 May.

blocks.text: The following passages are taken from an interesting lecture given by the Revd Father Eduardo Pereira and published in Funchal’s *Diario de Noticias* on 22 and 23 July 1941.

‘The social life of Porto Santo is also a subject of interest, curiosity and study because of the striking contrast it presents with that of Madeira. Its people have always remained isolated within the island and within their own ethnicity, customs and traditions.

It is a distinctive and original land within the archipelago’s geological and demographic make-up. Its people, descended directly from two races, Portuguese and Arab, display their influences and ancestral traits in everything.

They are Portuguese in the strongly marked traits inherited from the colonisers of the 16th century, and Arab in ancestral features of pronounced Moorish character. The former reveal themselves in concerns over caste and in moral attributes; the latter in physical characteristics and dispositions born of intermixture. In their moral formation, however, the people are more distinctly Portuguese. The island and its inhabitants display such physical and political affinity with mainland Portugal that one might readily say they belong more there than here. The education of those people is itself another distinctive facet of considerable psychological significance.

Their way of life and feeling, social relations, notions of hygiene, qualities of courtesy and solidarity, language, family, paternal authority, marriage, pride of ancestry, morals, food, amusements, music and agricultural system – everything, absolutely everything – distinguishes the population of Porto Santo from that of Madeira. Out of Arab mistrust, the people neither give nor open themselves to anyone at first contact, whether from the island or elsewhere, no matter where they come from. First they become acquainted with a person, then study them, and only afterwards esteem them with Portuguese frankness and affection. Their affection comes late but endures. No one should attempt to deceive them, for they will be the first to expose the deceit. Unusually intelligent and perceptive, they do not allow strangers to know them before they have first come to know those strangers. They nevertheless possess a captivating courtesy unrivalled among our populations’.

blocks.text: As is well known, Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) have the right to establish certain local legal provisions within their municipalities, in accordance with the country’s general laws. These provisions must be strictly observed, and their infringement incurs various penalties. Before 1834, it was not uncommon in this archipelago for these local codes or municipal by-laws (*posturas*) to conflict with decrees issued by the central government. This led the higher authorities to intervene forcefully and compel the municipal councils to comply fully with those decrees.
At various times, all the Councils in this archipelago established and enforced many ‘by-laws’, some of which were published in print.

As an attempt at ‘codification’, we know that in 1841, 1842, 1856, 1890, 1897 and 1900 respectively, the Municipal Councils of Santana, Calheta, Machico, Porto do Moniz, São Vicente and Ponta do Sol had their by-laws then in force printed as booklets. This was a sensible measure for good municipal administration.

In 1912, Funchal Municipal Council published the 245-page *Código de Posturas do Município do Funchal*, a collection of the by-laws then in force, the great majority of which remain in force today; the oldest dates from 1881. It is an excellent work of codification, specially compiled by the Council’s secretary, Luís Betencourt Miranda.

We face a great scarcity of information about this parish, beginning with uncertainty over the most reliable spelling of its name. The difficulty can be partly resolved by establishing precisely the origin of the word applied to that parish (*freguesia*). Does the name derive from *seixo*, meaning a stone or pebble beach (*calhau*), or from *seixo* as the name of a plant species? The latter meaning is generally accepted, on the grounds that the former is little known here, especially among the less educated classes. But would this also have been so in the earliest days of colonisation? It is worth recalling that, on the day after the first landing at Machico, the discoverers named a small beach Porto do Seixo. Today it belongs to the parish of Água de Pena, and was so named ‘because of what was found there’, says the historian of the islands. Modern dictionaries spell *seixo* the same way in both senses already mentioned, but older vocabularies use *seixo* for a pebble and *seiço* for a tree or plant. The name of the parish under discussion has been spelt in various, even outlandish, ways: Seisal, Seiçal, Seissal, Ceisal, Ceixal and Seixal. Some of these spellings are manifestly incorrect, but Seiçal is a correct, though antiquated, form and is also the one most commonly found in old documents. It would be both interesting and valuable to know how this word changed over a period of more than three centuries in the records of the relevant parish archive, but unfortunately we have been unable to investigate this. We believe that the name of this parish was taken from *Seixo* or *Seiço*, a small tree or shrub of the genus *Salix* and the family Salicaceae which, botanical publications say, ‘is found in stream beds and on many damp rocks in Madeira’. It was probably more widespread on the island at the time of its discovery and earliest settlement. We believe that the correct spelling to adopt would be Seiçal. However, since Seixal has been introduced and become generally established, it may now be pointless to oppose common usage, as many might regard this as a pretentious and ridiculous innovation.
